statement: In adults with moderate to severe anxiety related to a life-threatening illness, almost all with cancer (one randomized pilot trial at a single California clinic: 13 on MDMA, 5 on an inactive placebo), two MDMA sessions within manualized psychotherapy, compared with placebo with the same psychotherapy, were followed one month later by a larger fall in self-reported trait anxiety (STAI-Trait, scale 20 to 80: −23.5 vs −8.8 points; difference 14.7, 95% CI −0.5 to 29.9, editors' calculation; P = 0.056). The difference was not statistically significant and its interval runs from no difference to a very large one; the MDMA group started 5 points more anxious, and participants guessed their allocation correctly in 31 of 36 sessions. After the placebo group crossed over to MDMA, scores stayed lower at 6 and 12 months, with no control group left. The evidence is insufficient to say whether MDMA-assisted therapy reduces anxiety in people with a life-threatening illness. A Cochrane review of the same trial reached the same conclusion, with intervals it computed more conservatively (trait anxiety −14.7 points, 95% CI −29.45 to 0.05), and found no treatment-related serious adverse events (Schipper et al., 2024). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small trial, 18 adults with anxiety linked to cancer or another serious illness had talking therapy with either MDMA or a dummy pill. A month later, anxiety had dropped more in the MDMA group, but the difference could be chance, and most people could tell which pill they had.
population: Adults with a life-threatening cancer or non-dementing neurological illness (17 of 18 with neoplasms), life expectancy of at least 9 months, STAI-Trait of 45 or more and anxiety mainly related to the illness, off psychiatric medicines; excluded: ongoing first-line treatment such as initial chemotherapy, cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease, brain tumours, diabetes, psychotic and bipolar I disorders
exposure: MDMA in two blinded day-long sessions 2 to 4 weeks apart within manualized non-directive psychotherapy (three preparatory sessions and integration sessions after each)
comparator: Inactive placebo (lactose) with the same psychotherapy
outcome: Change in STAI-Trait from baseline to one month after the second session (primary); secondary anxiety, depression, sleep and well-being measures; uncontrolled follow-up to 12 months after crossover
magnitude: STAI-Trait change −23.5 (SD 13.2; n = 13) vs −8.8 (14.7; n = 5), P = 0.0558; Hedges' g 1.03, printed with a 95% CI of −5.25 to 7.31 that cannot be right (editors' approximate interval −0.05 to 2.12); raw difference 14.7 points, 95% CI −0.5 to 29.9 (editors' calculation, pooled t(16) = 2.06). Of 20 uncorrected secondary comparisons, only posttraumatic growth and mindfulness reached P = 0.04. After crossover, uncontrolled (n = 17): STAI-Trait 61.1 at baseline, 33.6 at 6 months and 34.2 at 12 months.

evidence.extracted: STAI-Trait change from baseline to one month after the second blinded session: −23.5 (SD 13.2) on MDMA vs −8.8 (14.7) on placebo, P = 0.0558; endpoint 38.9 vs 48.6; Hedges' g 1.03 printed with a 95% CI of −5.25 to 7.31. Editors' calculation: difference 14.7 points, 95% CI −0.5 to 29.9; approximate CI for g −0.05 to 2.12.
Placebo change scores ranged from −1 to −35 (median −3); excluding the one placebo participant with −35, a post hoc comparison gave P = 0.0066; the prespecified comparison gave P = 0.0558.
Baseline STAI-Trait 62.5 (7.3) on MDMA vs 57.4 (5.2) on placebo; history of PTSD 11 of 13 (84.6%) vs 2 of 5 (40.0%); the primary analysis compared unadjusted change scores.
At the end of each blinded session participants guessed their allocation correctly in 31 of 36 sessions (86.1%) and the co-therapists in 32 of 36 (88.9%).

Secondary outcomes at the primary endpoint: posttraumatic growth (P = 0.04) and mindfulness (P = 0.04) favoured MDMA; STAI-State (P = 0.10), BDI-II (P = 0.36), PSQI (P = 0.05), MADRS (P = 0.41), GAF (P = 0.52) and self-compassion (P = 0.21) did not differ significantly; no correction for about 20 tests.

After both groups had received three MDMA sessions (n = 17, no control group): STAI-Trait 61.1 (7.0) at baseline, 36.4 (9.5) at treatment exit, 33.6 (8.3) at 6 months and 34.2 (10.3) at 12 months; F(3,48) = 51.39.

evidence.extracted: All included trials were crossover trials; all outcomes after more than 3 months were measured after crossover, so no controlled long-term comparison is possible.

risk_of_bias.note: Participant-reported outcome with allocation evident; baseline imbalance with unadjusted analysis.

imprecision.note: Five controls; interval includes no difference.

grade.reasoning: One randomized trial: starts high. Risk of bias two levels (very serious, RoB 2 high for the measurement of the outcome): the primary outcome is self-reported while participants identified their allocation in 86% of sessions and expectancy was not measured; the MDMA group also started with higher anxiety and change scores were not adjusted for baseline, which could favour MDMA through regression to the mean. Imprecision two levels: 18 participants with only 5 controls, and the 95% interval of the difference runs from about −0.5 to 30 points. Indirectness not rated down because the claim is restricted to the trial population and endpoint. The relation is 'insufficient evidence' because neither an effect nor its absence is shown with precision.
